forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: East Sussex has approval in principle for £70.0m of exceptional financial support in 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
East Sussex County Council has received approval in principle for £70.0m of exceptional financial support (EFS), government permission to borrow to cover day-to-day spending, to balance its 2026/27 budget. Papers for its Audit Committee on 27 November say the budget includes planned use of £55.6m, with a £14.4m contingency. A council paper says reserves are at the minimum level required.

The papers say EFS is borrowing, not grant, so the council bears the financing costs. These are forecast at £1.8m in 2026/27 and £4.7m in 2027/28. One paper describes the borrowing as not sustainable and as adding future liabilities. The council already anticipates needing further EFS in 2027/28, with a current ballpark figure of over £100.0m.

Its external auditor, the accountancy firm Grant Thornton, has rated the council's financial sustainability red in its value for money report, its separate view of whether the council manages its money properly. It found one significant weakness, relating to the use of EFS. Its key recommendation asks the council to reduce reliance on EFS over time and to tell members the expected level, the reasons for it and the action taken. In its response, management says all efforts will be made to set a robust budget within continuing EFS, and that engagement with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and lobbying will continue.

news_drafts.headline: East Sussex pension fund auditor finds £6.2m valuation difference left unadjusted; note corrected by £26.1m
news_drafts.lead:
East Sussex's external auditor has identified a net understatement of about £6.2m (£6,168k) in the pension fund's Level 3 investments at 31 March 2026, which management is not proposing to adjust. The investments carry a balance of £1.15bn. The fund's total net assets in the final accounts are £5.28bn. The figures are in Appendix 1 to the Pension Board's papers for 6 November 2026.

The difference arose from timing: investment managers updated their valuations after the draft accounts were circulated. Management proposes leaving the financial statements unchanged. In the paper's words, "Management are proposing not to amend the financial statements on the basis that the differences are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively." The Audit Committee is to confirm this through the Letter of Representation.

The auditor also found that Note 26 to the accounts disclosed outstanding capital commitments of £246.2m, against an independently verified total of £220.1m, a difference of £26.1m. The auditor found the disclosed figure was an output error that did not match the supporting workings, treated the difference as non-trivial and recommended the note be updated. Management agreed to amend it.

news_drafts.headline: East Sussex asks government for up to £70m of exceptional support to cover a £55.6m 2026/27 deficit
news_drafts.lead:
East Sussex County Council has asked the government for permission to capitalise up to £70m of its spending to balance this year's budget, which carries a £55.6m deficit. The request, set out in the strategic risk register put to Cabinet on 29 September 2026, is for exceptional financial support (EFS): permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and a last resort. The government has agreed in principle.

The papers set out the terms. The support covers one financial year only and must be paid back. The council says it has told the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) that, without further government funding to address the underlying challenges, it is likely to need the support again for 2027/28 "to deliver our statutory duties". The register puts the cumulative deficit at £117.7m by 2028/29.

The risk register states the position in the council's own words: "Our revenue budget for 2026/27 includes a £55.6m deficit, which has led us to request Exceptional Financial Support from Government." Revenue budget here means the day-to-day running costs of services, as opposed to spending on things that last. The papers give no further breakdown of the deficit in the material reported here.

findings.headline: Reserves, assets and liabilities that will transfer with Fire and Rescue are still being confirmed and are not included in SBSA's reserves.
findings.detail: The transferring reserves, pension liabilities and other long-term commitments are being confirmed with East Sussex Fire Authority and West Sussex County Council. The position will be set out in the final budget report, and the same work will be done for other functions before they transfer.
findings.matters: Transferring pension liabilities and reserves are a balance sheet question that a lender or finance director would need to see before judging SBSA's financial position after the transfer.
findings.quote: pension liabilities and other long-term commitments, are being confirmed with East Sussex Fire Authority and West Sussex County Council

findings.headline: The Mayoral Capacity Fund grant of £2.8m in 2027/28 is an estimate based on the published formula, and will be confirmed in the local government finance settlement.
findings.detail: The grant is a key income line for SBSA's budget. Other recent government announcements, including the Autumn Budget capacity funding and Good Growth Fund money, are not yet built into the draft.
findings.matters: A finance director at another mayoral authority will want to know which grant lines are still estimates and which are confirmed, because the budget depends on these figures before the February settlement.
findings.quote: The Mayoral Capacity Fund grant of £2.8 million in 2027/28 is an estimate based on the published formula for newer mayoral authorities.

findings.headline: Transition costs are £0.83m in 2026/27 and £1.21m in 2027/28, against the £2 million estimated in the Quarter 1 report.
findings.detail: The paper describes these figures as broadly in line with the Quarter 1 estimate. Of the 2027/28 costs, £879k is funded, including £380k from the transition reserve set aside in 2026/27, and the remaining transition funding requirement is still to be reconciled.
findings.matters: A one-off transfer cost that has been estimated at £2m and is now being planned at a lower annual figure, with part of it funded from reserves, shows how a new authority is paying for its own set-up.
findings.figures: £0.83m in 2026/27; £1.21m in 2027/28; £2 million estimated at Quarter 1; £879k funded in 2027/28; £380k from transition reserve
findings.quote: Table 6 shows transition costs of £0.83m in 2026/27 and £1.21m in 2027/28, broadly in line with the £2 million estimated in the Quarter 1 report.

findings.headline: SBSA's draft revenue budget is balanced in every year of the Medium-Term Financial Plan to 2030/31, on current assumptions.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows total expenditure matched by income in every year, with net expenditure of zero. The paper notes that the position will be refined as funding allocations and the costs of transferring functions are confirmed.
findings.matters: A new strategic authority showing a balanced multi-year plan, while transferring functions and grant allocations are still unsettled, is a position other finance officers and lenders would want to compare with their own.
findings.figures: £52.9m SBSA draft expenditure in 2027/28; £93.2m in 2028/29; £91.3m in 2029/30; £91.4m in 2030/31; net expenditure nil in each year
findings.quote: The MTFP presents a balanced position to 2030/31 on current assumptions

findings.headline: East Sussex Fire and Rescue's draft budget shows a £1.1m gap in 2027/28, rising to £2.4m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: East Sussex Fire and Rescue has net expenditure of £56.5m in 2027/28 against funding of £55.3m. The service is preparing options to balance 2027/28, and further work is needed on later years.
findings.matters: An unbalanced fire budget transferring to a new fire authority, with no agreed closing measures, is a funding question that other councils and lenders would track before the February precept decision.
findings.quote: East Sussex has a £1.1m gap in 2027/28, and work is continuing to identify measures to balance the position before the final budget and precepts are set.
